chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'The mature/divorced woman proposes herself.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'She is the one most entitled to herself; she may entrust her affair to whomever she wishes, provided there is no objection to it, after she has previously married a husband.'

key_terms.أَمْلَكُ بِنَفْسِهَا: She is more entitled to herself / has autonomy over her person
key_terms.الثَّيِّبُ: A mature woman who has previously been married and consummated the marriage
key_terms.تَخْطُبُ إِلَى نَفْسِهَا: She proposes herself / manages her own marriage suit
key_terms.تُوَلِّي أَمْرَهَا: She entrusts her affair / manages her business
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no objection / it is permissible

ai.seo_question: Does a divorced or widowed woman need a male guardian for her marriage in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights the juristic distinction between a *thayyib* (mature woman with prior marriage experience) and a *bikr* (virgin), granting the former full autonomy to contract her own marriage without a mandatory male guardian (*wali*). It underscores the Shia scholarly view that her previous marital experience serves as sufficient proof of her judgment, allowing her to delegate the contract to any suitable representative of her choosing.
